options: A free, consensus-built hardening guide published by the Center for Internet Security for a specific OS or platform
A proprietary checklist written and sold exclusively by Microsoft
A single command that automatically hardens any Linux server with no review needed
A benchmark that only measures CPU and disk performance, unrelated to security
questions.explain: CIS Benchmarks are free, versioned documents built by a community of practitioners, covering most mainstream OS and platforms.

questions.q: What is the real difference between a Level 1 and a Level 2 CIS profile?
options: There is no practical difference — the levels are purely cosmetic labels
Level 1 is a broad, low-impact baseline meant for nearly every system; Level 2 is stricter defense-in-depth that may reduce functionality, reserved for higher-security environments
Level 2 is simply an older, deprecated version of Level 1
Level 1 only applies to Windows and Level 2 only applies to Linux
questions.explain: Level 1 recommendations have little to no impact on normal operation and apply broadly. Level 2 is stricter and intended for environments like those handling regulated data.

questions.q: What four things does a single CIS Benchmark recommendation include, beyond a one-line description?
options: Only a severity score and nothing else
A single shell command with no explanation of why it matters
A rationale, an audit procedure to check current state, a remediation procedure to fix it, and a mapping to the broader CIS Controls framework
A list of unrelated marketing claims about the vendor's product
questions.explain: A recommendation like 1.1.1.1 carries a rationale, an audit command, a remediation procedure, references, and a CIS Controls mapping — structured so it can be automated against.

questions.q: How does an engineer typically work through a CIS Benchmark in practice, rather than applying it recommendation by recommendation by hand?
options: By applying every single Level 2 recommendation regardless of the system's actual purpose
By ignoring the Benchmark entirely and relying only on antivirus software
By running a scanner such as OpenSCAP or CIS-CAT against a chosen profile, triaging the resulting failures, remediating real gaps, and re-scanning to confirm an improved compliance score
By memorizing every recommendation number and typing each fix from memory with no verification
questions.explain: Tools like OpenSCAP automate checking a host against a Benchmark's SCAP/XCCDF content, producing a pass/fail report an engineer triages and remediates against.

questions.q: In the lesson's example, why might a server's compliance score stay below 100% even after a thorough remediation pass?
options: Because compliance scores only apply to Windows systems, not Linux
Because the scanner always reports a random score regardless of actual configuration
Because CIS Benchmarks are impossible to ever fully satisfy on any system
Some failing recommendations are intentional, documented exceptions — such as a legacy app requiring a module the Benchmark wants disabled
questions.explain: Not every failing check should be fixed blindly — some gaps are kept open on purpose and documented with a justification for auditors.
